<reason>Both sides argued the motion as written and the clash narrowed cleanly to a single decision point: what a ministry should do when the only viable developer will not accept a price ceiling. B established that framing early (permission, not optimal contract design), used the leverage asymmetry (few fragile developers, non-credible buyer threat) to make refusal costly, and neutralized CON's strongest access material by pointing out that a high manufacturer price and nominal cost at the bedside are ordinary reimbursement design — turning A's hospital-budget scenario into an argument for the tool. B's Q1 was a genuine burden-exposing question, and A's honest "yes, walk away" answer became the hinge B pressed in closing, backed by an intuitive regret asymmetry (fiscal error vs fatal error) that A answered mostly by asserting that budgets also affect patients without dislodging B's point that reserve-antibiotic spend is a small line. A did real damage: the distinction between a large fixed reward and a high marginal price was the best idea in the debate, the "paying twice" and "equal expected revenue" pressure was sharp, and A caught a real tension between B's "paid whether it sits on the shelf" and "marginal courses are rounding error." But B's counter-turn — if total revenue really is equivalent, forbidding the high-unit-price variant costs nothing while risking the deal — left A defending a refusal whose upside was speculative. B's two clipped turns are an execution cost, though the decisive lines survived. B built the cleaner comparative route to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's reframe of A1.6: the hospital-affordability scenario is a product of unit-price purchasing, abolished by a central availability payment ("high price to the manufacturer and free at the bedside are entirely compatible"). Combined with the forced "walk away — yes or no" answer, this stripped A's access harm down to a national accounting concern that B's small-budget-line point largely absorbed.</best_rebuttal>
